paragraphs: Recovering an image from incomplete measurements requires assumptions about what plausible images look like. This paper studies an assumption supplied by an untrained neural network, rather than a handcrafted rule such as sparsity or a generative model trained on a large image collection. The image is modeled as belonging to the outputs of an untrained deep generative network with a fixed seed.

The authors consider both linear and nonlinear reconstruction problems. Their examples are compressive sensing and compressive phase retrieval. They introduce a projected gradient descent method that can be used in both settings and establish rigorous convergence guarantees. This connects a promising image reconstruction approach with an analysis of how an associated optimization algorithm behaves.

The paper also reports theoretical and empirical evidence that deep network priors can achieve better compression rates than handcrafted priors at the same image quality. The contribution therefore combines a reconstruction method, convergence theory, and evidence about measurement efficiency, within the stated network-based image model.
neurips-2019-algorithmic-guarantees-for-.tldr: An untrained network image model supports a reconstruction algorithm with convergence guarantees and evidence of improved compression at matched image quality.

paragraphs: Active learning chooses which unlabeled examples should receive costly labels. Standard probabilistic methods often make these choices greedily, selecting individual examples judged informative. At large scale, the paper argues, this process can become computationally impractical while producing only small changes in the model. Simply collecting individually attractive choices into a batch can also produce correlated queries.

The authors instead formulate Bayesian batch selection around approximating the posterior distribution over model parameters that the complete data would provide. This gives batch construction a collective target: choose a subset whose information represents the larger collection. Their algorithm produces diverse batches, addressing redundancy among the requested labels while supporting efficient active learning at scale.

For linear models, the approach yields interpretable closed-form solutions related to existing active learning procedures. Random projections extend the approach to arbitrary models. Experiments on several large-scale regression and classification tasks demonstrate benefits, supporting the usefulness of selecting informative batches jointly through a posterior-approximation perspective.
neurips-2019-bayesian-batch-active-learn.tldr: A Bayesian posterior-approximation approach selects diverse batches of examples for efficient active learning at scale.

paragraphs: A classifier can make accurate predictions yet provide unreliable estimates of how certain those predictions are. This distinction matters when deployment inputs differ from training inputs, for example because of sampling bias or changes over time. Useful uncertainty estimates should help indicate when a prediction deserves trust under these changed conditions.

The paper introduces a large-scale empirical benchmark of predictive uncertainty methods for classification under dataset shift. It covers Bayesian and non-Bayesian approaches and examines both prediction accuracy and calibration. Evaluating these together addresses two separate questions: whether predictions remain correct and whether the confidence attached to them remains informative as the data distribution changes.

The study finds that traditional calibration applied after training falls short under the shifts examined, along with several other existing methods. Some methods that average over models instead deliver surprisingly strong results across a broad range of tasks. These are comparative empirical findings: they identify promising uncertainty strategies while showing why strong predictive accuracy alone does not establish trustworthy confidence.
neurips-2019-can-you-trust-your-model-s-.tldr: A large classification benchmark finds that dataset shift undermines several uncertainty methods, while some model-averaging approaches perform strongly.

paragraphs: A multi-armed bandit learner repeatedly chooses among options with uncertain rewards. This paper adds structure by grouping those options into ordered categories. Its motivating example is online shopping, where a customer may prefer items from one identifiable category, even though the system initially does not know which category that is.

The authors introduce three progressively weaker ways to order categories, inspired by comparisons between random reward distributions. Stronger orderings impose more structure; weaker orderings accommodate a broader collection of bandit problems. For each model, the paper proves instance-dependent lower bounds on cumulative regret, measuring the unavoidable cost of learning instead of consistently choosing the best option.

These bounds explain how problem difficulty increases as the category assumptions become more general. The paper also supplies algorithms with theoretical guarantees that exploit the available ordering structure. An analysis of real data finds evidence that such ordered categories occur in practice, giving the mathematical setting an empirical motivation beyond the shopping example.
neurips-2019-categorized-bandits-c1463a6.tldr: Categorized bandits formalize ordered groups of options and provide algorithms and regret bounds showing how that structure affects learning.

paragraphs: When rewards are sparse, a reinforcement learning agent may experience too few successes to learn effectively. Hindsight experience replay helps by treating a state reached during a failed attempt as an alternative goal. The attempt then becomes useful evidence about accomplishing that alternative, even though it did not achieve the original objective.

This paper argues that the usefulness of these relabeled experiences changes as learning progresses. Its method, Curriculum-guided Hindsight Experience Replay, selects failed experiences using two considerations: how close their achieved states are to the true goals, and how much diversity they offer among alternative goals. The balance changes over training, emphasizing curiosity early and proximity to the intended goals later.

The resulting curriculum adjusts exploration and exploitation through the choice of experiences replayed, rather than treating all failures as equally valuable. The authors report improvements over the state of the art in challenging robotics environments. Those findings support adapting hindsight selection to the agent's learning stage.
neurips-2019-curriculum-guided-hindsight.tldr: CHER improves hindsight replay by gradually shifting experience selection from diverse alternative goals toward states closer to the true goals.

paragraphs: This paper studies a network of agents learning which options produce the best rewards. Each agent chooses an option and then communicates with its neighbors. The objective is to reduce the whole network's cumulative regret. The setting assumes that each option has the same reward distribution for every agent, with rewards drawn independently across agents and time.

The proposed algorithm shares information without a central coordinator. An accelerated consensus procedure lets agents estimate the average rewards observed throughout the network. These estimates arrive with delay and error, so the decision rule explicitly accounts for both when using upper confidence bounds to choose options.

The analysis bounds regret by the optimal centralized regret plus a term determined by the communication matrix's spectral gap. This separates the centralized learning benchmark from an additional network-related cost. The authors also provide a lower bound and report improved regret bounds, reduced requirements for network information, simpler analysis, and better empirical performance relative to prior approaches.
neurips-2019-decentralized-cooperative-s.tldr: A decentralized bandit algorithm combines consensus with delay-aware confidence bounds, achieving centralized regret plus a network-dependent term.

paragraphs: Variational inference approximates a posterior distribution by optimizing a more manageable distribution. Recent approaches use Monte Carlo likelihood estimators to construct tighter lower bounds on log-likelihood. However, a useful likelihood objective does not by itself explain which posterior approximation its optimization produces. That connection matters when the desired output is a distribution for inference.

The paper develops a procedure called divide and couple. Starting from a variational objective defined through a Monte Carlo likelihood estimator, it identifies augmented proposal and target distributions. The key result is an exact relationship: the gap between the objective and the log-likelihood equals a divergence between those augmented distributions.

This relationship gives the objective a distributional interpretation. Maximizing it reduces the associated divergence gap, linking objective improvement to approximation in the augmented formulation. After optimization, the augmented variational distribution may therefore be used to approximate the posterior. The contribution makes Monte Carlo variational objectives more directly useful for inference, beyond their role in estimating log-likelihood.
neurips-2019-divide-and-couple-using-mon.tldr: Divide and couple connects Monte Carlo variational objectives to posterior approximation by expressing their likelihood gap as a divergence between augmented distributions.

paragraphs: Machine learning systems can encounter inputs that differ from their training data without issuing any warning. This paper studies how to detect those distribution changes, show examples that characterize them, and assess whether they are harmful. These are related but distinct needs: noticing a shift does not by itself explain its nature or its consequences.

The authors compare methods across several datasets, changing both input-variable distributions and label distributions. They vary the strength of the changes and the fraction of examples affected. Across the shifts studied, the strongest detection approach combines dimensionality reduction through pretrained classifiers with a two-sample test, which compares whether two data collections follow the same distribution.

Methods trained to distinguish the source domains of examples serve another useful role. The study finds that they tend to help characterize shifts qualitatively and determine their harmfulness. The results therefore distinguish effective shift detection from useful shift diagnosis, providing empirical guidance for systems intended to make changing data conditions visible.
neurips-2019-failing-loudly-an-empirical.tldr: An empirical study identifies effective approaches for detecting dataset shift, describing its characteristic examples, and assessing whether it is harmful.

paragraphs: This paper asks how many examples suffice for neural networks with controlled weights to generalize. It considers networks of width d with sigmoid or smoothened ReLU activations, inputs in [-1,1]^d, constant-order spectral norm bounds, and Frobenius norm bounded by R. These assumptions define the network class covered by the result.

For any depth, the authors establish a sample complexity bound of order dR²/ε², up to logarithmic factors, where ε specifies the accuracy tolerance. This improves the previous d²R²/ε² dependence and is optimal up to logarithmic factors. A related bound controls deviations from reference weight matrices, allowing initialization-based guarantees that are sublinear in parameter count in many typical parameter regimes.

The proof introduces randomized approximate descriptions of functions. Roughly, if a function class admits descriptions using a given number of bits, that description budget controls the examples needed for uniform convergence: empirical and true losses remain close across the class. Tools for composing linear and nonlinear function classes make this principle applicable to the networks studied.
neurips-2019-generalization-bounds-for-n.tldr: Randomized approximate description length yields nearly optimal sample complexity bounds for specified neural networks with controlled weight norms.

paragraphs: Developing a machine learning model often also requires implementing an optimization solver. Repeating that engineering work across models has produced many specialized implementations. GENO investigates whether a broadly applicable optimization framework can reduce this burden while retaining the efficiency usually associated with carefully engineered, problem-specific solvers.

The framework combines a modeling language with a generic solver. Users declare an optimization problem, and GENO generates a solver for the corresponding problem class. The authors describe the framework as flexible enough to cover most classical machine learning problems. This makes the problem declaration the starting point for obtaining an executable solution method.

Across a wide variety of classical problems and some recently proposed ones, the generated solvers match well-engineered specialized solvers, exceed recent state-of-the-art solvers by a substantial margin, and outperform classical modeling-language-plus-solver approaches by orders of magnitude in the reported comparisons. These findings challenge the belief that generic optimization must sacrifice practical efficiency across diverse machine learning problems.
neurips-2019-geno-generic-optimization-f.tldr: GENO generates solvers from optimization declarations and reports efficiency competitive with or better than specialized approaches across varied machine learning problems.

paragraphs: A Markov chain describes a process whose next state depends on its current state through transition probabilities. This paper considers learning several such transition matrices from one observation stream per chain. The chains are assumed to be ergodic but are otherwise unknown, and the learner sequentially chooses which chain to sample.

The objective is to learn all transition matrices uniformly well according to a specified loss. The authors introduce a loss that extends squared error for distribution learning to Markov chains, then characterize what uniformly good performance means across problem instances. Their algorithm adaptively balances exploration and exploitation without requiring prior knowledge of the chains.

The analysis provides finite-sample, probably approximately correct guarantees, giving a probabilistic account of performance with a limited observation budget. It also proves that the algorithm approaches an optimal loss asymptotically. Together, these results connect the practical allocation question—which chain to observe next—with guarantees for both finite data and the long-run learning limit.
neurips-2019-learning-multiple-markov-ch.tldr: An adaptive sampling algorithm learns multiple unknown ergodic Markov chains with finite-sample guarantees and asymptotically optimal loss.

paragraphs: Expensive optimization becomes more difficult when several objectives compete. A hardware design, for example, may trade performance against energy use and area. The goal is to approximate the Pareto set of useful trade-offs while minimizing costly evaluations, rather than identifying a single design that is best on every objective.

The paper introduces Max-value Entropy Search for Multi-objective Optimization, or MESMO. Its acquisition function uses entropy in the output space to select the next input to evaluate. This turns uncertainty about objective outputs into a guide for deciding where to spend the next expensive measurement or simulation, with the aim of quickly uncovering high-quality solutions.

The authors provide a theoretical analysis characterizing the method's efficacy and evaluate it on synthetic and real-world benchmark problems. MESMO consistently outperforms state-of-the-art algorithms in those experiments. The stated findings support output-space entropy as a useful basis for allocating evaluations when the desired outcome is a collection of competing solutions.
neurips-2019-max-value-entropy-search-fo.tldr: MESMO uses output-space entropy to choose expensive evaluations and efficiently discover trade-off solutions in multi-objective optimization.

paragraphs: Multi-task learning seeks benefits from learning several tasks together. This paper extends that idea to tasks whose neural network architectures have no obvious overlap. The motivating question is whether models from very different domains can still share useful learned functionality, contributing toward more general problem-solving capabilities.

The approach decomposes architecture-and-task pairs into potentially related subproblems. An efficient stochastic algorithm then optimizes which parts should share functionality. Rather than requiring an obvious common architecture at the outset, the method discovers regularities, represents them as shareable modules, and combines those modules to support the individual tasks.

The authors first validate the approach on a standard synthetic multi-task benchmark, then apply it across vision, natural language processing, and genomics architectures. The reported results show that sharing modules across these domains improves individual task performance. This supports the feasibility of useful sharing across disparate architectures; the demonstrated contribution is a component relevant to future general problem solving, rather than a completed general-purpose solver.
neurips-2019-modular-universal-reparamet.tldr: A modular sharing method improves tasks across vision, language, and genomics even when their architectures have no obvious overlap.

paragraphs: Diplomacy combines cooperation and competition among seven players in a game without random events. Acquiring resources can require teamwork, trust, coordination, and betrayal. This makes it a setting for studying sequential social dilemmas in which cooperation may help players even though their interests do not fully align.

The paper focuses on No Press Diplomacy, which removes a dedicated communication channel between players. It introduces DipNet, a neural network policy model trained using a new dataset containing more than 150,000 human games. Supervised learning from expert trajectories first produces a playing policy. That policy then initializes a reinforcement learning agent trained through self-play.

Both the supervised agent and the reinforcement learning agent beat popular rule-based bots, demonstrating state-of-the-art No Press performance in the reported evaluation. The work contributes a gameplay model and a human-game dataset, while showing that expert imitation and subsequent self-play can produce strong policies in a multi-agent environment shaped by coordination and conflicting interests.
neurips-2019-no-press-diplomacy-modeling.tldr: DipNet learns No Press Diplomacy from human games and self-play, with both trained agents outperforming popular rule-based bots.

paragraphs: Planning becomes difficult when an environment changes while decisions are being made. This paper studies a setting where the agent knows the current environment model at each decision point but does not know how it will evolve. It assumes continuous change at a bounded rate, giving the planner some structure despite that uncertainty.

The authors formalize this setting as non-stationary Markov decision processes. Transition and reward functions satisfy a Lipschitz continuity condition with respect to time, which limits how rapidly they can change. Planning then treats the environment's possible evolution as adversarial, asking how to act under an unfavorable future consistent with the assumed regularity.

The resulting Risk-Averse Tree-Search algorithm, or RATS, is a zero-shot model-based planning method resembling Minimax search. Its worst-case perspective addresses uncertainty about future change rather than requiring that evolution to be known. Experiments illustrate its benefits and compare performance with reference model-based algorithms, grounding the proposed planning strategy in empirical evaluation.
neurips-2019-non-stationary-markov-decis.tldr: RATS plans against worst-case environmental change when the current model is known and transition and reward functions evolve at bounded rates.

paragraphs: Hyperbolic embeddings represent hierarchical relationships, such as synonym or type hierarchies, using points in hyperbolic space. Their numerical representation can become problematic: with ordinary floating-point arithmetic, standard Poincaré disk and Lorentz models have unbounded numerical error as points move far from the origin. This can limit the usefulness of an otherwise suitable geometry.

The paper proposes a representation based on an integer tiling of hyperbolic space. It proves a bound on numerical error for representing any point. The resulting model allows high-precision embedding learning without BigFloats and supports storing learned embeddings using fewer bits. Thus, the representation addresses both numerical accuracy and storage requirements.

Empirical evaluations demonstrate compression and improved embedding accuracy on real-world datasets. On WordNet Nouns, the reported compressed representation uses as little as 2% of the storage of a Poincaré embedding. That specific result illustrates the potential storage benefit, while the theoretical contribution concerns bounded numerical error throughout hyperbolic space.
neurips-2019-numerically-accurate-hyperb.tldr: An integer-tiling representation bounds hyperbolic embedding error and enables high precision and substantial storage compression.

paragraphs: Combining multiple input sources can improve predictions because the sources contain both complementary and shared information. Shared information might also help when one input becomes noisy. This paper investigates that possibility directly, focusing on robustness when noise affects a single source in a fusion model.

The authors first show that a linear fusion model does not automatically guarantee such robustness. They then propose two approaches for deep fusion: a deliberately designed loss with corresponding training algorithms, and a simple convolutional fusion layer whose structure offers an advantage in handling noise. These interventions address the training procedure and the fusion architecture, respectively.

Experiments on a deep fusion-based 3D object detector show that the training algorithms and the proposed layer provide robustness to noise applied to one source while preserving performance on clean data. The findings support explicitly designing fusion for this failure condition. They also establish why the mere availability of several inputs is insufficient to guarantee that shared information will protect predictions.
neurips-2019-on-single-source-robustness.tldr: Specialized training and a convolutional fusion layer improve a 3D detector's robustness to single-source noise while preserving clean-data performance.

paragraphs: Stochastic variance reduction has achieved strong theoretical and practical results in optimization. This paper examines whether that success carries over to training modern deep neural networks. The relevant setting involves difficult non-convex optimization, so the applicability of these techniques remains a question rather than a consequence of their success elsewhere.

The authors focus on straightforward applications of SVRG and related approaches. Their stated finding is that these naive applications fail, and the paper investigates why. The contribution is therefore an examination of a transfer problem: whether an established family of optimization techniques remains effective when applied to the training problems encountered in modern deep learning.

The scope of the conclusion matters. The finding concerns naive application of the studied methods, rather than establishing that every possible variance-reduction method must fail for neural networks. It challenges the expectation that prior optimization successes alone justify direct adoption in this setting and motivates understanding the source of the failure before treating these techniques as effective deep-learning optimizers.
neurips-2019-on-the-ineffectiveness-of-v.tldr: The paper finds that naive applications of SVRG and related variance-reduction methods fail in modern deep-network training and investigates why.

paragraphs: Identifying an unknown hypothesis can require choosing a sequence of tests, given a known distribution over possible hypotheses. This paper studies that decision-tree problem when some test outcomes are noisy. It includes persistent noise, where repeating a test for the same scenario returns the same noisy result, preventing repetition from resolving the uncertainty.

The authors develop approximation algorithms for two settings. Non-adaptive algorithms fix the test sequence in advance; adaptive algorithms choose later tests based on earlier outcomes. Their guarantees accommodate many noisy outcomes per test or hypothesis and degrade smoothly as that number increases. This extends previous work that assumed only a constant number of noisy outcomes.

The algorithms adapt methods from submodular ranking and stochastic set cover, obtaining nearly best-possible approximation guarantees. Evaluations cover toxic chemical identification and active learning of linear classifiers. Although the theoretical approximation guarantees are logarithmic, the reported solution costs are close to the information-theoretic minimum in these applications, showing strong practical performance within the evaluated settings.
neurips-2019-optimal-decision-tree-with-.tldr: New adaptive and non-adaptive testing algorithms handle persistent noisy outcomes with nearly best-possible approximation guarantees.

paragraphs: A set function assigns values to subsets of a finite collection. Its inputs are therefore indexed by the collection's powerset: the set of all possible subsets. This paper introduces convolutional neural networks designed for that structure, providing a way to define convolution when the underlying data organization consists of subsets.

The authors derive convolutions as linear functions that respect specified shifts on set functions. Shift equivariance means that shifting the input corresponds to shifting the output in the appropriate way. Their framework permits several notions of shift and includes a basic shift for each element of the underlying set, making its construction fundamentally different from graph convolutions based on a Laplacian.

The paper evaluates prototype powerset networks on several set-function classification tasks. These use synthetic data and data derived from real-world hypergraphs. The experiments demonstrate the potential of the proposed architecture. The central contribution is a structured definition of convolution for set functions, accompanied by initial classification evidence that the resulting networks can be useful.
neurips-2019-powerset-convolutional-neur.tldr: Powerset CNNs define shift-equivariant convolutions for data indexed by subsets and show promise on set-function classification tasks.

paragraphs: This paper studies learning representations without labels or end-to-end backpropagation. Its method uses the natural order in data to provide self-supervision. Motivated by the observation that biological networks appear to learn without a global backpropagated error signal, the authors divide a deep network into modules whose gradients remain isolated.

Each module learns locally to preserve as much information as possible from its inputs, using the InfoNCE bound as its training objective. Training is greedy in the sense that individual modules pursue their own representation objective. This raises a concrete question: whether locally trained stages can still build progressively more useful representations through the depth of the network.

The authors demonstrate that each module improves on its predecessor's output and that the top module produces highly competitive representations for downstream audio and visual classification. Gradient isolation also allows asynchronous optimization of modules, enabling large-scale distributed training of very deep networks on unlabeled datasets. The findings connect local learning objectives with useful final representations and a more flexible training arrangement.
neurips-2019-putting-an-end-to-end-to-en.tldr: Locally trained, gradient-isolated modules learn competitive audio and visual representations while enabling asynchronous training without labels or end-to-end backpropagation.

paragraphs: Continual learning requires a model to acquire tasks in sequence while retaining earlier knowledge. The paper notes that existing incremental methods lag behind models trained with all classes available together. RPS-Net addresses this setting by progressively selecting paths for new tasks while encouraging reuse and sharing of model parameters.

Its random path selection strategy avoids the overhead of computationally expensive evolutionary or reinforcement-learning-based selection methods. The model combines path selection with knowledge distillation and retrospection to address catastrophic forgetting. A controller dynamically balances plasticity, governing how the model accommodates new knowledge while maintaining previously acquired knowledge.

Extensive experiments report performance beyond the state of the art in incremental learning. The authors also state that, with parallel computation, the method can run in constant time with efficiency nearly matching a conventional deep convolutional network. That efficiency claim depends on parallel execution. Together, the results support path selection, retention mechanisms, and adaptive plasticity as a combined approach to learning from sequential tasks.
neurips-2019-random-path-selection-for-c.tldr: RPS-Net combines random path selection, parameter reuse, and retention mechanisms to improve incremental learning, with efficiency benefits under parallel computation.

paragraphs: Sparse image representations describe an image using a relatively small selection from a larger dictionary of components. Convolutional Sparse Coding uses filters that can appear at different image locations. Although this model has been useful in image processing, the paper notes that it has lagged behind traditional patch-based methods on tasks such as denoising.

The authors revisit how well the convolutional model represents natural images and suggest a Bayesian connection to its patch-based predecessor. Those observations motivate a supervised feed-forward network built around an approximation to minimum mean squared error estimation under the convolutional model. The architecture uses strided convolutions, linking its network design to the underlying estimation process.

The resulting architecture performs on par with state-of-the-art methods while using substantially fewer parameters, according to the reported results. The contribution therefore combines an examination of an image model with a practical network derived from that examination. It shows how reconsidering the relationship between convolutional and patch-based representations can lead to a competitive, parameter-efficient supervised architecture.
neurips-2019-rethinking-the-csc-model-fo.tldr: A Bayesian reconsideration of convolutional sparse coding motivates a supervised network that matches state-of-the-art performance with far fewer parameters.

paragraphs: Gradient-based optimization algorithms take discrete steps, but ordinary differential equations can describe related continuous-time motion. These descriptions can help explain learning dynamics and inspire algorithms. A difficulty is that, in the worst case, the discrepancy between an algorithm's steps and its differential-equation approximation grows exponentially with the number of iterations.

This paper studies a way to avoid that problem for Gradient Descent and Heavy-ball. Under additional regularity assumptions on the objective, the authors allow a small change to the algorithm's initial condition. With that adjustment, the corresponding continuous-time descriptions do not suffer from the stated exponential-error problem. Dynamical systems theory calls this behavior shadowing.

The analysis uses hyperbolicity and numerical analysis tools to establish the connection. Its significance is conditional: it supports continuous-time reasoning for the analyzed algorithms when the required regularity and initial-condition adjustment are allowed. It also changes the comparison being made, showing why nearby initializations can matter when relating discrete optimization trajectories to differential-equation models.
neurips-2019-shadowing-properties-of-opt.tldr: Under additional regularity, small initialization changes let Gradient Descent and Heavy-ball shadow continuous-time models without the stated exponential-error problem.

paragraphs: Batch policy optimization learns action choices from previously observed rewards. This paper examines cost-sensitive classification and contextual bandits, where the learner must generalize to unseen contexts without conducting exploration during the batch learning process. The central issue is how to choose a training objective that supports effective policy optimization.

When rewards for all actions are observed, the authors show that directly optimizing expected reward can encounter suboptimal plateaus and exponentially many local optima in the worst case. They construct a convex surrogate calibrated to entropy-regularized expected reward. This supplies an alternative objective with a formal connection to the reward criterion while addressing its unfavorable optimization landscape.

The paper then extends the surrogate to data where rewards are recorded for only some actions, yielding new objectives for batch contextual bandit training. The authors prove that the surrogate objectives remain sound in this partially observed setting and report state-of-the-art empirical performance. The contribution links improved optimization objectives with principled learning from incomplete reward feedback.
neurips-2019-surrogate-objectives-for-ba.tldr: Convex surrogate objectives address difficult reward-optimization landscapes and extend with theoretical support to batch learning from partially observed rewards.
